items.name: Failed ambush

Maip is the largest genus of megaraptorid known to date. We can imagine that we are dealing with one of the largest predators in its ecosystem.
On this occasion, an adult male fails in his attempt to hunt an isasicursor, which with its quick reflexes manages to evade the predator.
As today, success is not guaranteed for predators who take advantage of every opportunity to get food.

items.name: Futalognkosaurus dukei
items.description:
The African elephant is the largest terrestrial vertebrate that currently exists, and although other mammals have grown larger than others, the sauropods are much larger than any terrestrial animal in the history of life.
In the hemisphere, titanosaurs predominated, and we found very famous taxones like Argentinosaurus huinculensis or Patagotitan majorum.
And although the record of gigantic animals is fragmentary and rare, a large portion of animal species has been preserved, Futalognkosaurus poses all over its cervical vertebras (vertebras of the neck) and dorsal vertebras up to the frame, together with its sacral vertebras.

items.name: Oviraptor protecting its nest
items.description:
This animation, offers a glimpse into a hypothetical behavior of Oviraptor—often depicted as a nest raider due to its name (Latin: egg thief).
However, fossils tell a different story: the first specimen was found atop a nest, likely protecting it, not stealing from it. Modern research shows Oviraptor was likely a caring parent.
A great example of how scientific interpretations evolve over time.

items.name: Araripesuchus manzanensis
items.description:
A newly described species from the Cretaceous period, part of the Uruguaysuchidae family, named after the site "El Manzano" in La Buitrera, Argentina.
Unlike modern crocodiles, this group had relatively long limbs, suggesting they moved in a very different way—likely capable of running or galloping.
This artwork was created to celebrate its discovery.

items.name: Riojavenatrix lacustris
items.description:
Riojavenatrix lacustris is a newly described spinosaurid, published on February 19, 2024. Initially thought to belong to Baryonyx, the fossils revealed a unique combination of features that led to the naming of a new genus.
Its name means "lake huntress from La Rioja", referring to both its locality in Spain and its likely paleoenvironment. It is also one of the youngest known baryonychine spinosaurids in the fossil record.

items.name: The Lost World - 1925
items.description:
The Lost World (1925) is a landmark in the visual history of dinosaurs on screen.
Directed by Harry O. Hoyt and based on Arthur Conan Doyle’s novel, the film brought prehistoric creatures to life using groundbreaking stop-motion animation by Willis O’Brien — the same pioneer who would later shape King Kong. O'Brien worked closely with paleontologist Barnum Brown to ensure a degree of scientific realism, and his creature designs were deeply inspired by the paleoart of Charles R. Knight. The result is not only a milestone in cinematic storytelling, but also an early fusion of science, imagination, and visual art — setting the foundation for nearly a century of paleo-themed media to follow.
items.creditsLine: Directed by Harry O. Hoyt – based on Arthur Conan Doyle’s novel – produced by First National Pictures

items.name: Kostensuchus atrox
items.description:
After a long wait, the new crocodyliform discovered in the Chorrillo Formation, about 30 km southeast of the city of El Calafate, has finally been published.
Kostensuchus atrox is a new taxon that joins the family of Peirosaurids, a group of notosuchian crocodyliforms. It is a distant relative of the “Boar Crocodile” (Kaprosuchus).
The material corresponds mainly to the animal’s anterior region, with a very well-preserved and articulated skull, along with cervical and dorsal vertebrae, its pectoral and pelvic girdles, and both humeri.
"I want to thank @poldiego and @fernando.novas.5 for trusting me with this work and for all the valuable feedback that led to the result you see in the animation.
Congratulations to the whole team, and welcome Kostensuchus atrox!"

items.name: Spinosaurus | The Gathering
items.description: "Having the idea from seeing large quantities of crocodiles gathering for sunbathing, I thought to myself perhaps Spinosaurus could have exhibited similar behaviors. They are often depicted as solitary animal in paleo media, but the sheer size difference in adult and juvenile suggests to me Spinosaurus may have been very vulnerable to other large carnivores, which the Kem Kem formation had no shortage of, through out its life span and only become near untouchable once it is fully grown. Therefor Spinosaurus of various age and sizes may have gather in large groups, seeking safety from their numbers and the largest individuals in the herd. This video is my attempt at recreating this idea in #blender , using my latest #spinosaurus model."

items.name: Tyrannosaurus rex | Bone Bed
items.description: "The courtship behavior of modern birds are extremely diverse and unique. One bird in particular called the Bowerbird would build structures out of branches and decorate them with colorful objects to attract mates. This extraordinary behavior is what inspired me to make this 3D animation, with the male T.rex gathering skulls and bones of prey animals and lay them out in a mass display, making essentially a Bone Bed, to try and impress it's partner that it is a capable hunter. While also performing a "dance" that highlights it's strength and battle scars, hoping to be accepted and carry on the bloodline of one of the greatest predator in Earth's history."
items.freeTags: North America, Late Cretaceous, Tyrannosaurus rex, Triceratops

items.name: Triceratops | Lunch Time
items.description: "Every animal we have studied turns out smarter than we initially thought. In this video I want to show a speculative social dynamic in a herd of Triceratops, where more senior and larger individuals are respected. They also have strict rules and time-based behaviors that would not be tolerated if broken. Inspired by elephants herds, this animation aim to show the Triceratosp as a fascinating and socially complex animal.Want to learn how to animate with Blender? "

items.description: Every individual living life form are unique, and sometimes they are born with genetic mutations. And dinosaurs, the living and breathing animals they were, are no exception. Her skin itself was rare as it is, for her to survive till adulthood as well, was nothing short of a miracle.

items.name: ANTEDILUVIAN - Animation Short Film
items.description: The XIX century supposed a proggessive yet traumatic transition from the Old Regime to Modernity. Social movements, Technology, Literature, Art and Science were all at once changing how Humans perceive the world they lived in for ever. The very song that leads this motion picture was itself a game changer for music composition, just as the scientific discoveries that were happening at the time challenged society's world viewing. It was the begining of Paleontology . William Buckland notoriously tried to make sense of the Biblical dogma to the new scientific revelations. He theorized that the Antediluvian creatures that Mary Anning and Gideon Mantell were unearthing were probably punnished by God in a series of catastrophes, due to their apparent grotesque and violent nature, the Deluge being the ultimate one. The first dinosaur was formally described in 1824, exactly two centuries ago. Since then our perception of Megalosaurus has quite changed, and that's a reminder of how science progresses. This animated short is a commemorative homage to the pioneers who dared to stand for the truth they started to discover, considered 'outcasts' at the time; and the artists who for the first time imagined an entire different past of our planet.

items.description: Long before dinosaurs vanished, mammals were already adapting to dangerous conditions, developing unique strategies to survive in one of Earth's most hostile periods.

items.name: The Rise and Fall of the Tallest Mammal
items.description: Discover Paraceratherium, the largest land mammal to ever exist, tracing its evolutionary rise during the Oligocene and the environmental causes of its extinction.

items.name: How Ancient Art Captured Australian Megafauna
items.description: Aboriginal rock art in Australia may contain depictions of extinct megafauna like giant wombats and diprotodons, offering a unique window into prehistoric life.

items.name: How Dinosaurs Became Birds
items.description: Trace the evolutionary path from feathered theropod dinosaurs to modern birds, exploring the fossil evidence and biological mechanisms behind one of evolution's most remarkable transitions.

items.name: The Risky Paleo Diets of Our Ancestors
items.description: Explore what our prehistoric ancestors actually ate and the dangerous trade-offs involved in their dietary choices, from meat to toxic plants and risky scavenging.

items.name: How Humans Lost Their Fur
items.description: Investigate the evolutionary mystery of why humans lost their body hair, exploring the biological and environmental pressures that led to this unique adaptation.

items.name: The Neandertals That Taught Us About Humanity
items.description: Discover how the study of Neandertals, our closest extinct relatives, has transformed our understanding of what it means to be human.

items.name: How Prehistoric Men Survived
items.description: Explore the thrilling real story of life on Earth in prehistoric times, revealing how early humans adapted to extreme environments to survive against overwhelming odds.

items.name: Mothers Will Stop at Nothing to Protect Their Babies During Super Hurricane
items.description: 94 million years ago, during the Late Cretaceous, a super hurricane strikes the African coast as a mother pliosaur and a mother Spinosaurus fight to protect their young amid dying seas.
items.freeTags: North Africa, Late Cretaceous, Spinosaurus aegyptiacus

items.name: How Did the Dinosaurs Handle the Asteroid Hitting Earth?
items.description: 66 million years ago, a mated pair of Nanuqsaurus in the far north must survive the catastrophic aftermath of the asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs.
items.freeTags: North America, Late Cretaceous, Nanuqsaurus hoglundi

items.name: Ancient Gorgons Flee Deadly Pangea Fire
items.description: During the Permian mass extinction, a family of saber-toothed gorgonopsians flees a sweeping wildfire across Pangea, crossing paths with Scutosaurus and other Late Permian survivors.

items.name: Scutosaurus Stampede Kills a Mother; Ischigualastia Herd Flees a Flood
items.description: A Gorgon mother sacrifices herself during a Scutosaurus stampede to save her child, while an Ischigualastia herd navigates a two-year drought that ends in a deadly flood.

items.name: Baby Ischigualastia Narrowly Escapes Death in the Forest
items.description: During the Late Triassic, 232 million years ago, a baby Ischigualastia narrowly escapes death while its herd roams a rain-soaked Pangea.
items.freeTags: South America, Late Triassic, Ischigualastia jenseni

items.name: Dimetrodon, Early Permian, around 280 million years ago
items.description: Long before the dinosaurs, Dimetrodon dominated the terrestrial ecosystems of the Permian. This imposing synapsid, often mistakenly thought of as a reptile, is actually much closer to us on the tree of life than any dinosaur. This illustration depicts it at the edge of a stream, its large dorsal sail in orange hues catching the warmth of the morning sun. Below the water's surface, primitive fish move through a world just as fascinating.

items.name: Dunkleosteus terrelli, apex predator of the warm Devonian seas
items.description: A dive into the heart of the Late Devonian, around 370 million years ago, when Dunkleosteus terrelli reigned supreme over the oceans. This colossal placoderm, its head and thorax protected by articulated bony armor, had no true teeth: its jaws, formed of sharp, self-sharpening plates, could shear through almost anything in their path. The scene catches it exploring a reef carpeted with crinoids (sea lilies), sponges, and ammonites, while a jellyfish drifts silently in the diffuse light and another predator looms in the distance. A meticulously crafted paleoart reconstruction, faithful to the latest scientific knowledge, inviting viewers to rediscover the unsuspected richness of these primordial marine ecosystems.

items.name: Diplocaulus, one of the most iconic amphibians of the Permian
items.description: Resting on the sandy bottom of a shallow Permian stream, a magnificent Diplocaulus blends into its surroundings thanks to its mottled camouflage. Seen from a semi-aquatic viewpoint, the scene immerses the viewer in a world nearly 270 million years old, long before the appearance of dinosaurs. Its remarkable boomerang-shaped skull, one of the most distinctive anatomical features in the history of life, dominates the composition while schools of fish glide peacefully in the water above. Surrounded by giant horsetails, primitive ferns, and lush aquatic vegetation, the Diplocaulus waits patiently, perfectly adapted to its habitat.

items.name: Simosuchus and Beelzebufo, Madagascar, around 70 million years ago
items.description: In the heart of a tropical wetland of the Late Cretaceous, a massive Simosuchus rests on the shore while a Beelzebufo, the famous 'devil frog', silently watches its surroundings from the shallow waters. Surrounded by dense vegetation, tangled roots, and towering marsh plants, the scene captures a peaceful moment within a strange and fascinating ecosystem. Native to ancient Madagascar, these remarkable animals bear witness to the unique fauna that inhabited the island around 70 million years ago.
items.freeTags: Africa, Late Cretaceous, Simosuchus clarki, Beelzebufo ampinga

items.name: The Titanosaur scene in Jurassic World: Rebirth (2025)
items.description: For the release of the Jurassic World Rebirth DLC, my Instagram followers asked me to create fan art of certain scenes from the film. For this challenge, I chose to depict what I consider the most beautiful scene in the film: the Titanosaur scene, which stirs deep emotion. This fan art was created on Procreate.

items.name: Sinoceratops, China, 72 million years ago
items.description: This paleoart illustration transports the viewer into a lush forest of the Late Cretaceous, somewhere in present-day China. In the foreground, an imposing Sinoceratops drinks from a rocky, moss-lined stream, its broad head crowned with forward-curving horns that give the species its distinctive look, muzzle dipped into crystal-clear water. Its stocky body and blue-violet scaly skin stand out beautifully in the golden light filtering through the canopy. In the background, perched on a small rocky outcrop above a waterfall, a second adult watches over a juvenile, evoking a peaceful family moment typical of ceratopsian social life. The surrounding vegetation — tree ferns, cycads, and towering conifers — faithfully recreates the dense, humid ecosystem of Cretaceous Asia.

items.name: Mass Mating Under the Supermoon
items.description: A mass mating unfolds under the sea for coral, sea lilies, Sacabambaspis and orthocones during a supermoon event.

items.name: Mother Diplocaulus Protects Her Babies
items.description: During the Late Carboniferous period, swamp forests dominated much of the Earth. But with the threat of fires and drought on the horizon, how did vulnerable amphibians survive?
items.freeTags: North America, Late Carboniferous, Diplocaulus magnicornis

items.name: The First Primates Step Foot on Earth; Two Shark-Like Creatures Battle
items.description: Plesiadapis, the first primates on Earth, must find food in the forest to survive. Then, the changing ocean landscape changes the apex pecking order underwater.

items.name: The First Animals to Evolve a Backbone; The Age of Reptiles Begins
items.description: Meet the first fish with a backbone. Then, witness the dawn of reptiles.
